blocks.text: "A 30-year-old woman presents with difficulty conceiving. Take an appropriate history."

items: "Take a history from a couple with primary infertility."
"Take a history from a woman with secondary infertility."

blocks.text: "A couple has been trying to conceive for two years. Assess them."

items: "Take a history from a woman with recurrent miscarriage."

subsections.subsection_title: FIRST — CLARIFY WHAT THE PATIENT MEANS

blocks.text: Don't immediately start asking about menstrual cycles.
"Could you tell me more about your concerns regarding becoming pregnant?"

items: How long they have been trying
Whether they have ever conceived before
Whether either partner has previously had a child

blocks.text: For exam purposes, infertility is generally understood as failure to achieve pregnancy after a period of regular unprotected intercourse.
"I would establish the duration of regular unprotected intercourse and whether there has been any previous pregnancy."
Current definitions and thresholds can vary by guideline and patient circumstances, so avoid giving an unnecessarily rigid definition unless the examiner asks.
The couple has never achieved a pregnancy despite trying.
The couple has previously achieved a pregnancy but is now experiencing difficulty conceiving again.

items: "Why is it important to distinguish primary from secondary infertility?"

blocks.text: "Because the previous pregnancy provides information about previous fertility, and the differential causes and clinical history may be different."
C — Couple's presenting concern O — Ovulation/menstrual history U — Uterine/tubal factors P — Previous pregnancies L — Lifestyle/medical factors E — Evaluation of both partners
Duration → Previous pregnancies → Sexual intercourse → Female factors → Male factors → Previous investigations → Medical/surgical history → Lifestyle → Impact → Plan

items: "How long have you been trying to become pregnant?"
"Have you been having regular unprotected intercourse throughout that time?"
"How often would you say you have sexual intercourse?"
"Is intercourse timed around the middle of your menstrual cycle?"
"Regular vaginal intercourse capable of resulting in conception."
"What contraception were you using before trying to conceive?"

blocks.text: Now move into the female reproductive history.
Regular cycles make ovulation more likely, although they do not prove ovulation.
But don't rely on symptoms alone.
If there is irregular menstruation, think about:
"Have you ever been told that you have polycystic ovary syndrome?"
"Have you noticed any milk-like discharge from your breasts when you are not breastfeeding?"
Thyroid dysfunction can affect reproductive function.

items: "Have your periods become increasingly irregular or stopped?"
"Do you have deep pain during intercourse?"

blocks.text: "Do you experience pelvic pain that changes with your menstrual cycle?"
"Do you have pain when opening your bowels during your period?"
Endometriosis is an important cause of infertility.
"Have you ever been treated for a sexually transmitted infection or pelvic inflammatory disease?"

items: "Have you ever had an ectopic pregnancy?"

blocks.text: A previous ectopic pregnancy may indicate underlying tubal pathology and affects future pregnancy risk.

items: "Have you ever been diagnosed with fibroids?"

blocks.text: Even in "infertility," establish all previous pregnancies.
This helps distinguish primary vs secondary infertility and may reveal acquired reproductive problems.

items: "Have you ever become pregnant but subsequently lost the pregnancy?"

blocks.text: If recurrent pregnancy loss is the station, this becomes a much more detailed history.

subsections.subsection_title: MALE PARTNER — DO NOT FORGET HIM

blocks.text: This is one of the biggest OSCE points.
"Although we're discussing your fertility, fertility problems can involve either partner, so I'd also like to ask about your partner's health."

items: "Has your partner fathered a pregnancy before?"

subsections.subsection_title: MEDICATIONS AND EXPOSURES IN THE MALE PARTNER

items: "Does your partner use testosterone or anabolic steroids?"
"Do you take any regular medications or supplements?"

blocks.text: Both very low and high body weight can affect fertility.

items: "Have you had any investigations for fertility before?"
"Have you previously received any treatment to help you conceive?"
"How has the difficulty conceiving affected you emotionally?"

blocks.text: Infertility can have significant psychological and relationship consequences.
In many settings, infertility can carry substantial social pressure.
"Do you feel you have enough support from your partner and family?"
"Has anyone been putting pressure on you because you have not conceived?"
Do not assume that the woman is responsible.

"This is a 29-year-old woman who has been attempting conception with her partner for two years with regular unprotected vaginal intercourse. She has never previously conceived. Her cycles are irregular, occurring every 45–60 days, and she reports recent weight gain, acne and increased facial hair. She has no previous history of PID, pelvic surgery or ectopic pregnancy."
"Her partner has no previous children and reports normal libido and erectile and ejaculatory function."
"The history raises concern for an ovulatory disorder, particularly PCOS, although both partners require assessment."

"This is a 34-year-old woman who previously conceived spontaneously and delivered at term six years ago. She has now been attempting conception with her partner for two years without success. Since her previous pregnancy she has developed progressively painful periods and deep dyspareunia. She has no history of PID but had a previous pelvic surgery."

content_groups.group_title: "What are the main causes of infertility?"

blocks.text: "Broadly, infertility can result from female factors, male factors, combined factors, or remain unexplained. Female causes include ovulatory disorders, tubal and peritoneal disease, uterine pathology and reduced ovarian reserve. Male causes include abnormalities of sperm production, transport, sexual or ejaculatory function and hormonal disorders."

content_groups.group_title: "What is the first investigation you would request in the male partner?"

blocks.text: Don't order every possible test immediately.
"I would tailor investigations according to the history, examination findings, age, duration of infertility and previous results."
This sounds much more clinically mature.
"There are several possible causes, and sometimes both partners contribute. We would therefore assess both you and your partner rather than assuming the problem is coming from one person."
This is an excellent counselling statement.
A couple can report "trying" but have infrequent intercourse or difficulties with intercourse.
This determines whether the problem is primary or secondary infertility.
Tubal disease is an important cause of infertility.
Infertility is not purely a biological problem.
B — Both partners O — Ovulation T — Tubes/uterus H — History of previous pregnancy and sexual intercourse
Semen + Surgery + STIs + Lifestyle + Investigations + Treatment
If the examiner gives you very little time:

"How long have you been trying to conceive, and have you ever conceived before? Have you been having regular unprotected vaginal intercourse, and how frequently? What contraception were you previously using? Are your periods regular, and when was your LMP? Do you have dysmenorrhoea, deep dyspareunia, abnormal bleeding, symptoms of PCOS or symptoms suggesting thyroid or prolactin disorders? Have you had previous PID, STIs, ectopic pregnancy or pelvic surgery? Have you had previous fertility investigations or treatment? I'd also like to ask about your partner's previous fertility, sexual function, testicular problems, medical history, medications including testosterone or anabolic steroids, and lifestyle factors such as smoking, alcohol and drug use."
That is an excellent high-yield infertility station answer.
